As of 240 AM EST Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Rain is expected across portions of the area today, 
although amounts will generally be light. Locally higher totals are 
possible across far southern VA and northeast NC.

This morning, developing low pressure is located off the Carolina 
coast with a secondary area of low pressure off the coast near the 
FL/GA border. Very light rain has started to stream into far 
southern portions of the area. The main forecast challenge today 
continues to revolve around how these lows will develop and where 
they will track. The latest guidance has continued to converge 
toward a more offshore solution, with the primary coastal low 
becoming dominant while the weaker inland low gradually dissipates. 
As a result, the associated precipitation shield is expected to 
remain less expansive than earlier guidance suggested, with much of 
the heavier rainfall likely remaining south and east of the local 
area. 

The majority of the latest CAMs as well as the 00z GFS and RRFS 
continue to show a substantially drier solution across much of 
central and eastern VA with generally light QPF amounts. The 00z 
ECMWF has also trended considerably drier across VA compared to 
previous cycles, although it continues to depict a more organized 
inland band of rain extending NE from the Carolinas into far 
southern VA. Some of the latest high res guidance also does at least 
hint at locally higher amounts across northeast NC and around the 
VA/NC border. 

Given the increasingly consistent guidance trends, QPF has been 
lowered across much of the forecast area, with most locations 
expected to receive around 0.25" of rain or less. However, as 
mentioned, locally higher totals potentially around 1", cannot be 
ruled out across interior northeast NC and adjacent far southern VA 
if a more persistent inland rain band develops. Confidence in the 
placement of these higher amounts remains relatively low. 

Rain chances will continue to increase form south to north 
throughout this morning, with the best opportunity for rain 
generally during the late morning and afternoon before tapering off 
later this evening into tonight. Some lingering light rain remains 
possible along the immediate coast into early Monday morning. 
Temperatures today will remain mild with highs generally ranging 
from the mid 60s to lower 70s. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier and milder conditions return Monday, followed 
by cooler weather Tuesday. 

Low pressure continues to quickly move northeast and away from the 
Mid Atlantic coast Monday. Meanwhile, a dry cold front will be 
crossing the area during the day on Monday. High pressure builds 
back into the area later Monday through Tuesday. Temperatures remain 
mild on Monday due to downsloping flow in the wake of the front, 
highs will range from upper 60s to lower 70s. Cooler air arrives 
Tuesday as that high builds southward from eastern Canada. Dry 
weather is expected throughout the day, but clouds may gradually 
thicken, especially by Tuesday night. Highs on Tuesday will only 
stay in the 50s area-wide, with lows dropping back into the mid-
upper 20s to lower 30s inland and mid 30s to lower 40s along the 
coast.


KEY MESSAGE 3...A potentially more impactful coastal storm could 
bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding Wednesday into 
Thanksgiving Day. Specific impacts remain uncertain.

Attention turns to a potentially more significant coastal storm 
developing during the middle of the week. While uncertainty remains 
regarding the exact track, strength, and timing of the system, the 
latest 00z GFS and ECMWF continue to depict low pressure developing 
off the Southeast coast Wednesday before strengthening and tracking 
northward near the Mid Atlantic coast Wednesday night into 
Thanksgiving Day. Of particular note is the strong area of high 
pressure, possibly exceeding 1040 mb, situated over eastern Canada 
and the Northeast ahead of the approaching coastal low. The pressure 
gradient between the two features could support a prolonged period 
of strong NE winds along the coast (and over the waters). Both the 
GFS and ECMWF depict the fairly strong coastal low by Thanksgiving 
Day, although differences remain regarding exact track and inland 
extent of the precipitation shield.

The latest 00z EPS continues to also support the potential for a 
more impactful storm, particularly near the coast. Probabilities of 
wind gusts exceeding 34 knots are relatively high along the 
immediate Atlantic coast. The EPS also depicts a notable heavy 
rainfall signal with ~20 to 40% probabilities of exceeding 2" of 
rainfall in 24 hours across portions of the forecast area, generally 
higher closer to the coast. This suggests that while widespread 
heavy rainfall remains far from certain, the potentially for locally 
significant amounts is at least possible. Of potentially greater
